passage: At the June festival in their town square in Brazil, Paulo loved the man in the bright clown hat. The man smiled, gave Paulo a sweet, and said, "Come see the puppies behind the van." Paulo took a step. Leila, the grey-aproned lady at the corn stall, called, "Paulo, wait!" He hid behind a post; her plain face and loud voice scared him. Leila held his hand firmly and walked him straight to Mamãe. Mamãe hugged him tight and told the festival guard about the man. That night she said, "Nice smiles don't mean safe. Safe grown-ups bring you back to me."

qa.q: What did the man offer to show Paulo?
qa.a: The puppies behind the van.

qa.q: Why did Paulo trust the man in the clown hat but hide from Leila?
qa.a: The smile and the sweet made Paulo feel happy and safe, while Leila's plain face and loud voice made him nervous, so his feelings decided for him.

qa.q: What did the adults do right?
qa.a: Leila took Paulo straight to Mamãe, Mamãe told the festival guard at once, and that night she taught him that safe grown-ups bring you back to your parent.

qa.q: How might Leila have felt when Paulo hid from her?
qa.a: She was probably alarmed for his safety and maybe a little hurt, but she acted anyway, holding his hand and bringing him to Mamãe.

grounding: A young child trusts a friendly-seeming stranger because it feels good and fears a plain-looking helper because she makes him nervous.

passage: At the preschool Diwali party, a shiny box of bright pink sweets sat on the gate wall. Nobody knew who had left it. Chetan reached for one. "They look yummy, so they're good!" The new helper, Kashish didi, in her plain brown sari, gently moved the box away. Chetan stepped back, nervous; she didn't smile much, and her voice was deep. But she knelt and offered him a laddoo from the class tray. "These are from your teacher's kitchen. Those, we don't know." Chetan took it slowly. At pickup, the teacher told all the parents about the unknown box.

qa.q: Where was the shiny box of sweets?
qa.a: On the gate wall.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel nervous of Kashish didi?
qa.a: Her plain sari, few smiles and deep voice made him uneasy, so his feeling said she wasn't safe even though she was helping him.

qa.q: What rule did Kashish didi show?
qa.a: Eat food from people we know, not food from an unknown giver, however nice it looks; she explained it kindly and offered a safe laddoo.

qa.q: What is it like for Kashish didi when Chetan steps back?
qa.a: She may feel a little sad at seeming scary, but she stays gentle and kneels to his level.

grounding: A young child judges sweets as safe because they look nice, and a plain-looking helper as scary because he feels nervous.

passage:
Monday, a cold winter morning: Tarun cries at the bus stop. The new attendant, Jatin bhaiya, is tall and unsmiling, with a scratchy voice. "Scary!" Tarun says.
Wednesday: At the park, a smiling man in a cartoon sweater offers Tarun a toffee. Tarun beams and reaches out. Mumma steps in, says, "No, thank you," and takes Tarun home. She tells the park guard that afternoon.
Saturday: Mumma plays "safe or not" with Tarun. "Who helped you with your bag on the bus?" "Jatin bhaiya." "Do we know him?" "Yes!" "And the toffee man?" Tarun thinks. "Smiley, but we don't know him."

qa.q: What did the man in the cartoon sweater offer Tarun?
qa.a: A toffee.

qa.q: Why did Tarun call Jatin bhaiya scary?
qa.a: Tarun felt nervous because Jatin bhaiya was tall and unsmiling with a scratchy voice; the feeling made him seem unsafe even though he helped.

qa.q: What helped Tarun learn?
qa.a: Mumma stepping in at the park, telling the guard that afternoon, and playing "safe or not" to link safety to knowing someone, not to smiles.

qa.q: What might Jatin bhaiya feel when Tarun cries at the bus stop?
qa.a: He might feel a bit hurt or awkward, though he keeps helping Tarun with the bag.

grounding: A young child feels a smiling stranger is safe and a plain-looking helper is scary, until a parent helps him sort it out.

passage: In the harvest weeks after Baisakhi, the village school let out early so children could help in the fields. Walking home past the wheat stacks, Baljeet told his friend Zubin, "Science is easy. And useful! I'll be a tractor engineer." "And grammar?" "Grammar is hard and useless. Who needs it?" Zubin laughed. "You got nine out of ten in grammar yesterday. And you failed the science quiz." Baljeet kicked a clod of earth. He had already forgotten the grammar mark. Science just felt good, so it felt easy. Grammar felt boring, so it felt pointless. "Well," he muttered, "grammar is still boring."

qa.q: What did Baljeet score in grammar yesterday?
qa.a: Nine out of ten.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet think science is easy?
qa.a: He enjoys science, so it feels good and easy, while boring grammar feels hard and pointless; his liking supplies the answer, not his marks.

qa.q: What could help Baljeet judge subjects more fairly?
qa.a: Look at the real marks, the nine out of ten and the failed quiz, and ask what each subject is useful for, not only how it feels.

qa.q: How does Zubin see Baljeet's opinion?
qa.a: Zubin finds it funny and points to the marks, seeing clearly what Baljeet's feelings hide.

grounding: A boy thinks the subject he likes is easy and useful and the one he dislikes is hard and pointless, whatever his marks say.

passage: On Lucia morning, Anders' school in Uppsala was full of candles and singing. Holding his trumpet, Anders told his friend Mateo, "Music is the easiest subject, and the most useful. You can play anywhere!" "What about maths?" "Maths is impossible. And pointless. When will I ever need fractions?" Mateo tilted his head. "You use fractions in music. Half notes, quarter notes. Mr Berg said so." Anders opened his mouth, then closed it. Half notes. He had counted them all morning without any trouble. "That's different," he said. "That's fun." Mateo grinned. "Maybe maths is fun when it's music."

qa.q: What does Mateo say Anders uses in music?
qa.a: Fractions: half notes and quarter notes.

qa.q: Why does Anders call maths impossible and pointless?
qa.a: He dislikes maths, so it feels hard and useless, while music feels fun and therefore easy; his feelings are answering for him.

qa.q: What could help Anders see maths differently?
qa.a: Noticing where he already uses it, like counting half and quarter notes, and judging a subject by what it does, not only by how it feels.

qa.q: How does Mateo view Anders' claim?
qa.a: Mateo sees the link Anders misses and teases him gently, perhaps hoping Anders will enjoy maths more.

grounding: A boy judges his favourite subject easy and useful and his disliked one hard and pointless, though he uses both.

passage: During the summer term, the school timetable had two new periods: swimming and library. Harsha loved swimming. "It's easy, it makes you strong, and nothing bad can happen," he told Noor Ma'am, the library teacher. "Library is hard. And useless. It's just sitting." Noor Ma'am raised an eyebrow. "Nothing bad can happen at the pool? Then why is there a lifeguard?" Harsha shrugged. "That's for babies." "And the story about the lost fisherman last week? You told me the whole plot." Harsha frowned. He had loved that story. "That was different. That was exciting." Noor Ma'am smiled. "So maybe library is exciting sometimes, and swimming needs care sometimes."

qa.q: Who is at the pool, according to Noor Ma'am?
qa.a: A lifeguard.

qa.q: Why does Harsha say nothing bad can happen at the pool?
qa.a: He loves swimming, so it feels safe and good, and that liking pushes the risks out of mind; library feels boring, so it feels hard and useless.

qa.q: What could Harsha do to judge more fairly?
qa.a: Look at facts, like why the pool has a lifeguard and how much he enjoyed the fisherman story, before deciding what is risky or useful.

qa.q: How might Noor Ma'am feel when Harsha calls library useless?
qa.a: She may feel amused and a little stung, but she stays patient and uses his own reading to show him.

grounding: A boy sees the activity he loves as risk-free and useful and the one he dislikes as hard and pointless.

passage:
"The ramp jump is totally safe, Ritu didi. Everyone does it."
"Mridul, the boy from B-block broke his wrist on that ramp last month."
"He was doing it wrong. It's fun, so it's fine."
"Okay. And the olympiad trip to Delhi? With two teachers, on a train?"
"That's dangerous. Trains, crowds, strangers. No way."
"Which one has actually hurt someone you know?"
"...The ramp. But the trip feels scary."
"And the ramp feels exciting. That's your gut talking, not the facts."
"So what, I skip the ramp?"
"Wear pads and a helmet, like Papa said. And think about the trip again tomorrow."
"Fine. But I'm still nervous about Delhi."
"Nervous is allowed. Just don't let it decide on its own."

qa.q: What happened on the ramp last month?
qa.a: The boy from B-block broke his wrist on it.

qa.q: Why does Mridul think the ramp jump is safe?
qa.a: It feels fun and exciting, so it seems low-risk, while the trip feels scary, so it seems dangerous, even though the facts point the other way.

qa.q: What does Ritu suggest?
qa.a: Wear pads and a helmet as Papa said, and think about the trip again tomorrow, so feelings don't decide alone.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel during this talk?
qa.a: She is probably worried about his safety but patient, trying to show him the facts without mocking him.

grounding: A teenage boy judges a thrilling ramp jump as safe and a well-supervised trip as dangerous, going by feelings rather than facts.

passage: Last year I judged everything by how it felt in my stomach. Riding on the back of my cousin's scooter without a helmet felt thrilling, so it felt safe. Standing up in the inter-school debate, the only boy on our team, felt terrifying, so it felt like the riskiest thing I could do. My aunt Vandana asked me once, "Gautam, which one could actually hurt you?" I laughed it off. Then my cousin skidded on gravel one evening, not badly, but his elbow was a mess, and I saw the helmet rule differently. The debate, meanwhile, went fine; I even won a prize. Now when something feels exciting, I ask what could go wrong. When something feels scary, I ask what could go right.

qa.q: What happened at the inter-school debate?
qa.a: It went fine, and Gautam even won a prize.

qa.q: Why did riding without a helmet feel safe to Gautam?
qa.a: It felt thrilling, and the excitement made it seem low-risk, while the debate felt terrifying, so it seemed dangerous.

qa.q: What habit does Gautam use now?
qa.a: When something feels exciting, he asks what could go wrong; when something feels scary, he asks what could go right.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt when Gautam laughed off her question?
qa.a: She was probably worried about his safety and a bit frustrated that he didn't take it seriously.

grounding: A teenage boy judged risk by thrill and fear until a real skid and a good debate showed him the facts.

passage: Coach's note, athletics camp. Yogesh wants to try the high dive at the town pool this weekend without any training because it "looks awesome", yet he refuses to run the 400 metres because it "feels scary", though he trains for it daily and is quick. When I asked what the actual risks were, he couldn't name one for the dive and listed five for the race. His teammate Indu said, "You love the dive, so it looks safe." I told Yogesh the dive is off until the pool's diving coach trains him, and I called his mother today to explain. We will try the 400 on Monday, one lap at a time.

qa.q: How many risks did Yogesh list for the race?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: Why does the high dive look safe to Yogesh?
qa.a: It looks awesome and exciting, so his liking makes it seem low-risk, while the race feels scary, so it seems dangerous despite his training.

qa.q: What did the coach do, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Put the dive off until a diving coach trains him, told his mother the same day, and planned the 400 one lap at a time, matching choices to facts.

qa.q: How does Indu see Yogesh's thinking?
qa.a: Indu sees clearly that he loves the dive and that is why it looks safe, and says so in a way he may hear more easily from a teammate.

grounding: A teenage boy judges a thrilling dive as safe and a race he fears as risky, going by feeling rather than facts.

subtype: Gut feeling on people and products [Actor]
passage:
"So why this laptop?" Bhavna asked, turning the box over. "It costs more than the one we compared."
"It just felt right the moment I held it."
"Okay, but why?"
"The keyboard. Better keyboard."
"Yesterday you said the other keyboard was nicer."
"Battery, then. Longer battery."
"Same battery. It's on the sheet."
Dhruv looked at the comparison sheet he had made himself, still on the table. "Screen?"
"Same screen, Dhruv." She laughed. "You liked the silver colour, didn't you?"
He grinned, caught. "Maybe. I'm finding reasons afterwards, aren't I?"
"Just a bit. It's fine if you love the colour. Just say that."
"Okay. I love the colour. And I'll take it back tomorrow while I think again."

qa.q: What did Bhavna say about the battery?
qa.a: It was the same battery, and it was on the sheet.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv keep offering new reasons?
qa.a: He felt drawn to the laptop, probably by the silver colour, and is a bit embarrassed, so he builds reasons after the choice to justify the feeling.

qa.q: What would you advise Dhruv now?
qa.a: Admit the feeling, check it against his own comparison sheet, and take a day before deciding, as he plans to.

qa.q: How does Bhavna experience the conversation?
qa.a: She is amused rather than critical, gently testing each reason until he sees the pattern himself.

grounding: A student picks a product because it feels right and then invents reasons afterwards.

subtype: Gut feeling on people and products [Actor]
passage: When I was choosing a flatmate last year, I met Lavanya for ten minutes and just knew. Her laugh, her plants, the way she made chai. I told my sister I had picked her because she seemed "responsible and quiet". My sister laughed: "Hafsa, you chose her for the plants." Honestly, I had no idea if she was either; I found those words later, to sound sensible. The other applicant, whom I felt nothing for, had sent references and a clear message about rent. Lavanya turned out lovely, but also loud, and late with bills twice. I don't regret it. But I've learned to notice when my gut picks first and my head writes the speech afterwards. Now I ask: what would I say if I hadn't already decided?

qa.q: What had the other applicant sent?
qa.a: References and a clear message about rent.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa describe Lavanya as "responsible and quiet"?
qa.a: Hafsa felt instant warmth toward Lavanya and wanted to sound sensible, so found those words afterwards to justify a gut choice.

qa.q: What question does Hafsa ask now, and why does it help?
qa.a: "What would I say if I hadn't already decided?" It separates the feeling from the reasons so both can be checked.

qa.q: How might the other applicant have seen Hafsa's choice?
qa.a: They might feel disappointed and puzzled, having sent references and a clear message, without knowing a gut feeling decided it.

grounding: A young adult chooses a flatmate on gut feeling and builds the reasons afterwards.

subtype: Gut feeling on people and products [Actor]
passage: Placement officer's note, Tuesday. Varun came in to accept the offer from the smaller design studio. When I asked why, he said it "just felt right" after the office visit: the plants, the music, the friendly receptionist. Then he added reasons: better growth, better projects. When I asked which projects, he couldn't name one. His classmate Pankaj, who had the same offer, had asked the studio for a sample contract and spoken to two current employees. I suggested Varun do the same before signing, and treat his good feeling as one piece of information. He agreed to email the studio today.

qa.q: What did Varun like about the office visit?
qa.a: The plants, the music and the friendly receptionist.

qa.q: Why couldn't Varun name the projects?
qa.a: His choice came from a warm feeling during the visit; the "better projects" reason was added afterwards, so he felt sure without evidence.

qa.q: What did the officer suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Ask for a sample contract and talk to current employees before signing, treating the good feeling as one piece of information.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Varun's reasons?
qa.a: Pankaj, who checked the contract and spoke to employees, might see Varun's reasons as thin, even if the studio turns out to be good.

grounding: A student picks a job because it feels right and supplies the reasons afterwards.

passage: The contract had to be signed by five, and it was already four. Hafsa sat across from Kiran, the new supplier, and felt a tightness in her stomach. Something about his quick smile made her want to say no. She noticed the feeling and named it silently: uneasy. Then she asked herself what the evidence said. She opened his file: three references, all positive; two years of on-time deliveries; one billing dispute, settled. Nothing matched the unease, except that he talked fast, like a cousin she didn't trust. "Give me ten minutes," she said, and called one reference herself. The reference was warm and specific. Hafsa signed at 4:40, the tightness gone.

qa.q: How many references were in Kiran's file?
qa.a: Three references, all positive.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when Kiran smiled?
qa.a: She felt uneasy, with a tightness in her stomach, partly because he talked fast like a cousin she didn't trust.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's steps would you copy?
qa.a: Naming the feeling, then checking the file and calling a reference herself before deciding, even with the deadline close.

qa.q: What would have changed for Kiran if Hafsa had simply trusted her gut?
qa.a: He would have lost a contract over a feeling that came from someone else, despite a good record.

grounding: A thoughtful adult notes her uneasy feeling, treats it as information, and checks the evidence before signing.

passage: The flat in Bandra had a sea breeze and a window seat, and Sudha fell for it in thirty seconds. "This is the one," she whispered to her friend Siddharth, who had come along to help. Then she caught herself. "I'm excited," she said aloud. "That's a feeling, not a fact." She took out her notebook. For: light, a short walk to the station, the window seat. Against: the broker wouldn't show the lease, a damp stain under the sink, and the rent was higher than the other two she had seen. "The excitement is real," Siddharth said. "So is the damp." Sudha smiled. "I'll ask for the lease and come back on Saturday before I decide."

qa.q: What did Sudha list against the flat?
qa.a: The broker wouldn't show the lease, there was a damp stain under the sink, and the rent was higher than the other two.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when she first saw the window seat?
qa.a: She felt excited, falling for the flat in thirty seconds, then caught herself and treated the excitement as information rather than proof.

qa.q: What did Sudha decide, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To ask for the lease and come back on Saturday before deciding, so the facts can be checked against the feeling.

qa.q: How does Siddharth support her?
qa.a: He respects both sides, saying the excitement is real and so is the damp, which helps her think without feeling dismissed.

grounding: An adult notices her excitement about a flat, treats it as information, and checks the facts before acting.

passage:
"I have a bad feeling about the Bengaluru offer, Aparna."
"Bad how?"
"Just... heavy. Like I'd be making a mistake."
"Okay. Is the feeling about the job, or about moving?"
Binita paused. "Maybe moving. Leaving Maa. Leaving you."
"So what do the facts say about the job?"
"Better team. Better work. The manager I spoke to seemed decent."
"And what says no?"
"Long hours in the first months. And... I'd be alone."
"So the heaviness might be missing us, not the job being wrong."
"Maybe. It still counts, though."
"Of course it counts. It's information. Talk to someone who works there, and visit the city once before you decide."
Binita let out a long breath. "Okay. Feeling noted. Facts next."

qa.q: Which city is the offer in?
qa.a: Bengaluru.

qa.q: What might Binita's heavy feeling be about?
qa.a: It may be sadness and worry about leaving Maa and Aparna, rather than a sign that the job itself is wrong.

qa.q: What next steps does Aparna suggest?
qa.a: Talk to someone who works there and visit the city once before deciding, treating the feeling as information to check.

qa.q: What is it like for Aparna to hear Binita's worry?
qa.a: Aparna seems caring and calm, taking the feeling seriously while helping sort it from the facts, and is perhaps touched that missing her is part of it.

grounding: An adult treats a heavy feeling about a big decision as information and asks what evidence supports or contradicts it.

passage: Class note, Holi party. When the colour trays came out, Minakshi grabbed the whole green tray before anyone else could. Sahil reached for it too, and Minakshi pushed him, fast, without a word. Then she ran off to the slide, green hands and all. When I brought her back, she looked surprised, as if the grab and the push had happened on their own. We practised "freeze, breathe, ask" together, and she asked Sahil, "Can I have green after you?" He said yes. I told her mother at pickup, and we will play freezing games next week.

qa.q: Which tray did Minakshi grab?
qa.a: The whole green tray.

qa.q: How did Minakshi seem when the teacher brought her back?
qa.a: She looked surprised, as if the grab and the push had happened by themselves; she acted on her first impulse without thinking.

qa.q: What helped Minakshi slow down?
qa.a: Practising "freeze, breathe, ask" with the teacher, which led her to ask Sahil for a turn.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt when he was pushed?
qa.a: Sahil was probably startled and upset, then pleased when she asked nicely and he could say yes.

grounding: A preschooler grabs, pushes and runs on first impulse with little pause to think.

passage: At the Pongal fair in the village, Jeevan saw a red balloon floating near the tea stall across the road. He let go of his sister Minakshi's hand and ran. A bullock cart creaked closer. Minakshi grabbed his shirt just in time. "Jeevan!" Appa scooped him up. Jeevan wriggled. "Balloon!" He had not seen the cart at all; he had only seen red. Appa held him close and said, "Stop, look, then walk. Say it with me." Jeevan said it, sniffing. Then Appa bought the red balloon and tied it to Jeevan's wrist.

qa.q: What did Jeevan see near the tea stall?
qa.a: A red balloon.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan run across the road?
qa.a: He was excited about the balloon and acted on his first impulse; he hadn't even seen the cart, only the red.

qa.q: What did Appa teach Jeevan?
qa.a: "Stop, look, then walk", a simple pause to practise before moving.

qa.q: What might Minakshi have felt when she grabbed his shirt?
qa.a: She was probably frightened for him and then relieved that she caught him in time.

grounding: A preschooler runs toward a balloon on first impulse, with no pause to notice the cart.

passage: On the first snowy morning in their Istanbul courtyard, Elif built a tiny snowman, and Sami knocked its head off with one swipe. Elif cried. Sami looked at his mitten, then at the snowman, then at Elif. He hadn't planned it; his arm had just moved. Anne came out, knelt in the snow, and said calmly, "Hands stay still first. Then we think." She counted to three with him, slowly. "Now, what can you do?" Sami scooped up snow and patted a new head onto the snowman. Elif sniffed, then pressed in two pebble eyes.

qa.q: What did Sami knock off?
qa.a: The snowman's head.

qa.q: What does Sami's look at his mitten suggest?
qa.a: He seems surprised and unsure, even a bit sorry; he hadn't planned it, his arm just moved on impulse.

qa.q: How did Anne help Sami?
qa.a: She stayed calm, taught "hands stay still first, then we think", counted to three with him, and asked what he could do to fix it.

qa.q: How might Elif feel when Sami rebuilds the snowman's head?
qa.a: She is still a little upset but comforted enough to join in, adding two pebble eyes.

grounding: A preschooler swipes on impulse without thinking, and a parent helps him add a pause.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Winter holidays, day three. At breakfast Keerthana akka gave me a riddle: "A bat and a ball cost 110 rupees together. The bat costs 100 more than the ball. How much is the ball?" I shouted "10!" straight away. Akka just smiled and said, "Check it." If the ball is 10, the bat is 110, and together they're 120. Wrong! I was so annoyed. Then I tried again slowly: ball 5, bat 105, together 110. YES. Akka says the first answer always jumps out and feels right. My new trick: count to three and check before I shout. I got her next riddle right! 🙂
Sachin

qa.q: What was Sachin's first answer?
How did Sachin feel after finding the first answer was wrong?
qa.a: Sachin felt annoyed at first, then pleased and proud after checking slowly and getting 5.

qa.q: What is Sachin's new trick?
qa.a: Count to three and check before shouting an answer.

qa.q: How does Keerthana akka see Sachin's quick answer?
qa.a: She expected it, knowing the first answer jumps out, and helps by saying "check it" instead of giving the answer away.

grounding: A child learns that a quick answer to a trick question can feel right but be wrong, and that a pause to check helps.

passage: On the threshing floor after Eid, Irfan and his cousin Ankita sat on sacks of paddy, waiting for the tractor. "Riddle," said Ankita. "How many months have 28 days?" "One! February!" Irfan said at once, already grinning. Ankita raised her eyebrows and waited. Irfan's grin slipped. His teacher always told the class to take a breath when a question seemed too easy. He took one. January had 31 days, so it had 28 days too, and more. "Wait... all of them," he said slowly. "All twelve." Ankita laughed and clapped. Irfan felt the pleasure of catching himself, better than being fast.

qa.q: What was Irfan's first answer?
qa.a: "One! February!"

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after catching himself?
qa.a: He felt pleased and proud; catching himself was a better feeling than being fast.

qa.q: What helped Irfan find the right answer?
qa.a: Remembering his teacher's advice to take a breath when a question seems too easy, then checking.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Irfan corrects himself?
qa.a: She is delighted, laughing and clapping, glad he worked it out himself.

grounding: A child catches a wrong first answer to a trick question by pausing to think.

passage: At summer camp near Valencia, the children sat in the shade of an olive tree while Beatriz, the counsellor, handed out riddles. "In a race, you overtake the runner in second place. What place are you in now?" Bilal's hand shot up. "First!" Beatriz tilted her head. "Are you sure? Take three breaths." Bilal breathed, picturing the track. He had been behind the second runner, then in front. The first runner was still ahead. "Second," he said, cheeks warm. "I'm in second!" "Why did first come so fast?" she asked. Bilal thought. "Because it felt like winning."

qa.q: What did Beatriz tell Bilal to take?
qa.a: Three breaths.

qa.q: Why did the answer "first" come so fast to Bilal?
qa.a: It felt like winning, so the exciting first answer felt right; after correcting it he felt a bit embarrassed, with warm cheeks.

qa.q: What could Bilal do with future trick questions?
qa.a: Picture the situation and take a few breaths before answering, especially when an answer comes very fast.

qa.q: What is it like for Beatriz to watch Bilal work it out?
qa.a: She is probably pleased that her question and the three breaths let him reason it out himself, without her giving the answer.

grounding: A child learns to pause and catch a fast but wrong answer to a trick question.

passage: Teacher's note, science fair week. In the lab on her own, Manjula is careful: she checks each measurement twice and writes down her reasons. But at lunch today, with friends watching, she agreed on the spot to swap her tested project for Lavanya's flashy volcano, "because everyone laughed and said it was cooler". By the afternoon she looked worried. I asked her to write out both ideas on paper, calmly, as she does in the lab. After ten minutes she decided to keep her own project and help Lavanya with the volcano on the side. We talked about pausing when the group is loud.

qa.q: What did Manjula agree to swap her project for?
qa.a: Lavanya's flashy volcano.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel by the afternoon?
qa.a: She looked worried, sensing that the quick lunch decision, made with friends laughing, didn't fit her careful reasoning.

qa.q: What helped Manjula decide well?
qa.a: Writing out both ideas calmly on paper, as she does in the lab, which let the slow, careful way of thinking take over.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel about Manjula's final decision?
qa.a: Lavanya might be a little disappointed, but glad of the help with the volcano on the side.

grounding: A teenager makes a snap choice with friends watching and careful choices when calm.

passage:
Friday night.
Two versions of me today. Morning, maths test: calm Alka. Read every question twice, checked my working, changed one answer that looked right but wasn't. Evening, at Aadhya's birthday: everyone shouting "Truth or dare, Alka!" and I picked dare before I even thought, then agreed to post a video of myself dancing badly. It's already up.
